title: Why I Make My Kids Talk to Strangers (or the Unexpected Board Game)
author: Kevin Stinehart
summary: Stinehart explains that he and his wife make their daughters talk to cashiers, waiters and clerks so that they come to believe from experience that most people are good. Following Lenore Skenazy, he distinguishes teaching children to recognise danger from teaching them that danger is everywhere. He cites eBay's founding premise that most people are honest, falling crime, the rarity of stranger abduction and research linking overprotective parenting to child anxiety, including Ortiz's Independence Therapy. He ties the argument to a community Playbrary, a free park cabinet of play materials, whose first days brought a donation rather than theft. He argues for being hopeful without being naive and for trusting both neighbours and children.
points: Everyday exchanges with strangers give children first-hand evidence that most people are decent.
Perceived danger has drifted from the evidence, and overprotection is associated with greater childhood anxiety.
Independence-focused activities can reduce anxiety, so more opportunity rather than more protection helps.
The Playbrary experiment shows trust in a community and in children inventing their own rules, accepting modest losses as a reasonable cost.
quotes: But there’s an enormous difference between teaching children how to recognize danger and teaching them to assume that danger is everywhere all the time.
We want our daughters to grow up believing that most people are good.
And here’s the troubling part: Our perceptions of danger have become disconnected from the evidence.
Research has found that overprotective parenting is associated with greater childhood anxiety.
Frequently helping children become less anxious, isolated, and worried may require giving them more opportunities to experience the world, not fewer.
The relevant question isn’t whether every item will always be returned. It’s whether the benefits to children outweigh the relatively modest costs of keeping the Playbrary stocked.
Instead of focusing exclusively on the situations children fear, he helps them discover that they’re capable of navigating the world independently.
